Colombian filmmaker Juan Sebastián Mesa and Salvadoran director Tatiana Huezo were two of the big winners last night at the San Sebastián Film Festival’s industry awards. **Scroll down** to see the full list of award winners.

Mesa won the WIP LATAM Industry Award with his latest project, _Lovers Go Home!._ The film follows Alejandra, a single mother who works as a webcam model in a studio in Medellín, and Andrew, a disabled war veteran living in the outskirts of New Jersey. They begin a series of online conversations that range from sexual propositions to trivial challenges, forging a connection that starts with physical intimacy but evolves into a sweet complicity. The official synopsis continues: “Their loneliness clashes when he decides to travel to meet her in person. What begins as an unpleasant encounter eventually becomes an opportunity for them to question who they truly are.”

Mesa is best known for his debut feature, _Los nadie_ (2016), which won the Audience Award at Venice Critics’ Week. He has also directed the short films _Kalashnikov_ (2014) and _Tierra mojada_ (2017). _Lovers Go Home!_ was selected for the 2022 Co-Production Forum at San Sebastián.

Huezo won the EGEDA Platino Industria Award for the best WIP Latam with her film _Galerna._ The film follows Lúa and Noé, who are tasked with casting non-professional actors for a science fiction film. Working together for the first time, Noé, who comes from a rural background, is skeptical that Lúa, an unemployed actress from the city, is the right person for the job. The official synopsis continues: “Together, they travel to remote locations and make their home in the houses of farmers who take them in. Immersed in an unfamiliar reality, they discover a Mexico that embraces them but also confronts them with their own fears and prejudices, testing their tolerance, resilience, and vulnerability.”

Huezo**’**s first feature, _The Smallest Place_ (2011), won the Ariel Award for Best Mexican Documentary and was included in the _4+1: Contemporary Mexican Cinema program at_ San Sebastián. In 2016, she debuted _Tempest_ in the Forum section of the Berlin Film Festival. The film received the Ariel Awards for Best Director and Best Documentary and was nominated for the Goya Award for Best Ibero-American Film. In 2023, her film _The Echo_ won the Best Director and Best Documentary awards in the Encounters section of the Berlin Film Festival.

The insult was architectural: one cell, three bodies, a shelf for each man, a bucket, cold seeping through masonry. On 2 March 1949, in Warsaw’s Mokotów Prison, Kazimierz Moczarski – a former officer of the Polish Home Army falsely charged as a collaborator by the communist regime – was pushed into a room with two Germans. One was Gustav Schielke, an ex-policeman and Nazi functionary. The other was  SS-Gruppenführer Jürgen Stroop, liquidator of the Warsaw Ghetto.

“My shock at finding myself with Nazis,” Moczarski writes, “quickly transformed into a resolution: if I am now with war criminals, then let me get to know them, try to break down the threads of their life stories and personalities.” If he succeeded, he might have an answer to his question: what “historical, psychological, sociological mechanism” had led some Germans to join “a gang of mass murderers who governed the Reich”?

## The flight to Hamburg sparked concern on Wednesday evening after declaring an emergency mid-air
**Bethan Finighan** Science and Innovation Writer and [**Kirstie McCrum**](https://www.walesonline.co.uk/authors/kirstie-mccrum/) Deputy Head of News, Live News Network
An [EasyJet](https://www.walesonline.co.uk/all-about/easyjet) aircraft bound for Germany executed a dramatic mid-air U-turn, returning to Manchester after declaring an emergency above the North Sea.
Flight EZY32GY, travelling from Manchester to Hamburg, raised alarm on Wednesday evening (September 23) after issuing an in-flight emergency declaration and reversing course near Amsterdam.

According to Flight Radar, the aircraft departed at 7.15pm — one hour and 15 minutes behind its scheduled take-off time — before squawking 7700 and turning back roughly 30 minutes after becoming airborne.

Squawk 7700 is the universally recognised aviation transponder code employed by pilots to indicate a general in-flight emergency, reports [the Manchester Evening News](https://www.manchestereveningnews.co.uk/news/greater-manchester-news/manchester-easyjet-flight-makes-sharp-34662913).
Real-time aviation alert service Squawk posted on X shortly after 8pm: "An AIRBUS A-320 (EZY32GY) is squawking 7700 - declaring an emergency at 34,000 ft near Amsterdam, Netherlands."
EasyJet confirmed the flight diverted back to [Manchester Airport](https://www.walesonline.co.uk/all-about/manchester-airport) owing to "a technical issue with the aircraft".
The airline stated that emergency services were on hand to meet the plane upon landing "as a precaution only", and issued an apology to passengers for the disruption caused to their journeys.

An EasyJet spokesperson said: "Flight EZY2195 from Manchester to Hamburg this evening returned to Manchester due to a technical issue with the aircraft. The aircraft was met by emergency services as a precaution only and customers disembarked normally.
"Due to Hamburg Airport's curfew restriction the flight was delayed overnight and will continue the journey on 24 September.

"We are very sorry for the inconvenience caused and did everything possible to minimise the impact of the delay. While we always look to secure hotel accommodation, as there was very limited availability, we advised customers they would be reimbursed for booking their own.
"The safety of its passengers and crew is easyJet's highest priority and easyJet operates its fleet of aircraft in strict compliance with all manufacturers' guidelines."

Kelly Brosch

SOUTH LAKE TAHOE, Calif. – As a young girl who spent her summers in the Al Tahoe neighborhood of South Lake Tahoe, little did Kelly Brosch know that her old stomping ground would lead to her passion and her livelihood.
And now, Kelly is celebrating 20 years of owning her store, GaiaLicious Global Gifts. She will be celebrating that milestone with a two-day party, September 25 and 26 (see schedule below).

The San Francisco native spent the summers of her childhood in South Lake Tahoe at her family’s second home. After going away to college at Long Beach State, where she majored in marketing, Kelly lived in Southern California for a while after graduation, then traveled to Europe and settled in Germany when she met her husband Felix. They married in 1997 and spent the next 11 months backpacking through Southeast Asia. She returned to the United States with Felix in 1998 and bought her parents’ house, the same one she had spent her summers in.

Kelly worked different jobs over the next eight years in South Lake Tahoe, including substitute teaching and working at the store, Maison Rustic. During her and Felix’s time in Asia, she started seeing what she wanted to carry in her own store, a dream she’d had for years. During a walk in her neighborhood, she saw a storefront for rent on Tallac Avenue that was the perfect size for her plans, and GaiaLicious Global Gifts was born.
Her two daughters, now 23 and 27, grew up in the store their parents created.

Kelly says the area surrounding the store was perfect from the beginning – the restaurants, shops, and other businesses make it a great place for the shop. She enjoys the customers who are locals, second homeowners, and out-of-towners.

It hasn’t always been easy to get to the 20th anniversary – weather is always a challenge with wind, snow and shoveling, and power outages. There were the fires and COVID. The weather does help bring people in when they are escaping the 100-degree days in the valley.
She supports local artists, follows trends, and highlights “shop local,” all things customers appreciate.

But with challenges, surprises also come. Kelly says the support from the community was a welcome surprise when she opened her doors. When her husband Felix died of cancer in 2024, the community supported Kelly and her family through food, hugs, and funds.

At some point, Kelly said she would retire and sell the store. Her mom is 100 years old and lives in Placerville, and she’d like to travel more and enjoy her daughters and “bonus daughter,” who has two children.
In the meantime, it is celebrating its first 20 years. For more information on the store and hours, visit [https://www.gaialicious.com/](https://www.gaialicious.com/).

## Bundestag set for organ donation debate
The Bundestag will discuss two separate cross-party proposals on Thursday to increase the number of human organs donated for often life-saving transplant operations.
One proposal upholds Germany's current system, under which people who wish to donate organs must actively give permission.
Advocates of the proposal say that the shortfall of donated organs can be remedied by campaigns calling on adults to take part and making it easier to register the desire to donate.
The other proposal calls for an opt-out scheme under which organs can be removed postmortem from anyone who has not expressly rejected being an organ donor.
Backers of this proposal say that although surveys show that most people in Germany are willing to donate their organs, very few actually document this wish.
They also cite statistics showing that countries with opt-out schemes have more donations, with Germany lagging behind in international comparisons.
Altogether 254 of the 630 members of the Bundestag have signed on to the opt-out scheme, and 58 have backed the first proposal to maintain the current national system.
The Bundestag last voted on the issue in 2020, with a majority supporting the opt-in model, even though an opt-out proposal had more signees then, too.
France, Spain and the Netherlands are examples of European countries that have opt-out models in place.

[Germany](/en/germany/t-17871182) has [presented a roadmap](https://www.bundesumweltministerium.de/download/deutschlands-roadmap-fuer-die-schrittweise-abkehr-von-fossilen-energien "External link — presented a roadmap") to phase out [fossil fuels](/en/oil-gas/t-19021263) by 2045.
Germany's Environment Minister Carsten Schneider told the UN General Assembly on Wednesday that the plan "combines independence, affordability, and climate protection."

Europe's largest economy is now the third country to have provided a solid plan for the phaseout — to which nearly 200 countries committed at the 2023 COP28 climate conference in Dubai — following France and the Netherlands.
## What did Berlin say about the fossil phaseout plan?

Schneider, of the center-left Social Democratic Party, said the decision was linked to the [Iran war](/en/iran-war/t-76168615) and its [impact on fuel supplies](/en/iran-wars-economic-impact/t-76891279) worldwide.

"It is not just extreme weather events around the world that demonstrate how urgently we need to do more to protect the climate," he said. "If the situation in the Strait of Hormuz determines whether [people can still afford their daily commute](/en/germany-eyes-heat-pumps-as-iran-war-drives-energy-costs-up/a-77310083) to work, that is not a good state of affairs."
## Germany's chemical industry hit by high energy prices

He said he believed the 19-year deadline was feasible.
"Our roadmap is intended to set an international example. I am sure that many other countries will follow."
Schneider said that fossil fuels accounted for 65% of Germany's energy consumption in 2024.

The majority of that — 98% of its oil and 95% of its natural gas — was imported at a cost of €76 billion ($86.5 billion). The minister stressed that the figure has since risen sharply due to the Iran war.
## How have environmental organizations reacted to the plan?

Several environmental organizations welcomed Berlin's plan, though some highlighted that it [contradicted some recent government decisions.](/en/germany-to-adjust-heating-law-to-allow-fossil-fuels/a-76252944)
"With this announcement, Germany is showing a sign of life in international climate policy," said Greenpeace energy expert Mira Jäger.
However, she noted that "at the same time, the federal government is subsidizing the oil industry, breaking the heating transition, and slowing down the expansion of renewables."
## How does natural gas harm the environment?

Fentje Jacobsen, a climate policy advisor at the World Wide Fund for Nature, argued that the roadmap largely rehashed existing initiatives without adding "new ideas or additional ambitions."
"The current government is meanwhile planning to rely less on renewables and more on gas," she added.

Energy Minister Katherina Reiche of the conservative Christian Democrats has advocated building new gas-fired power plants, arguing that this would help stabilize the electricity grid and highlighting the intermittent nature of renewable sources such as wind and solar.

Reiche has also demanded preserving a larger role for combustion-engine vehicles using alternative fuels, a position that contradicts the phaseout plan, which foresees battery-electric cars accounting for 100% of new passenger car registrations by 2035.

Following state [elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin](/en/elections-in-berlin-and-mecklenburg-western-pomerania/t-79320225), two of Germany's 16 federal states, the mood within the center-left [Social Democratic Party](/en/social-democratic-party-spd/t-17437818) (SPD) is oscillating between relief and frustration, confidence and bewilderment.

"The SPD is clearly capable of winning more than 30% of the vote," party co-leader [Lars Klingbeil](/en/lars-klingbeil/t-72438206) said jubilantly in Berlin. "This result in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is an encouragement for the entire Social Democratic movement."

As Klingbeil put it, [Manuela Schwesig](/en/can-mecklenburg-western-pomerania-premier-schwesig-stop-far-right-afd-winning-state-election/a-79264225), the SPD state premier of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and her party had shown "how to make up ground, how to fight, and how, with the right issues and the right approach, to stage a comeback and ultimately win people over through that effort."

What Klingbeil conveniently omits is that Schwesig's success was also because she distanced herself as much as possible from the federal government's policies, and by extension from the SPD at the national level, which it governs in coalition with the center-right CDU/CSU alliance of the [Christian Democratic Union](/en/christian-democratic-union-cdu/t-17351950) and its Bavarian sister party, the [Christian Social Union](/en/christian-social-union-csu/t-17439619) under Chancellor [Friedrich Merz](/en/friedrich-merz/t-60575802).
